01 / HOW I THINK

Good AI isn't just about what it can do.
It's about what it shouldn't.

I care about the moment after a model responds. Is the output valid? Is the action allowed? Is the evidence strong enough? And if it isn't — does the system know how to stop?

That thinking shapes the systems I build: structured outputs, deterministic policy checks, privacy controls, evaluation suites and human review paths. The model contributes intelligence. The surrounding system earns trust.

I also care about the people using the workflow. An automation is only useful when it removes friction without hiding responsibility.

01 — INSURTECH / CLAIMS AUTOMATION

OPD Claim Engine

An AI claims assistant for employee health bills. Employees submit a bill; the pipeline extracts and audits it. Clean, small claims can move forward instantly. Doubtful cases go to human review. Money decisions stay with fixed rules and the database — not the LLM.

Engineering details: FastAPI publishes jobs to Kafka; workers extract with Groq, validate strict Pydantic schemas, apply policy checks, mask PII and create a HubSpot handoff when needed.

01 / OPD CLAIM ENGINE · EVENT-DRIVEN PROCESSING

How do you stop slow AI inference from taking down the upload API?

Bill uploads, extraction latency and policy checks have different execution times. Running the full pipeline inside the request path couples user experience to model availability.

REQUEST PATH → ASYNC WORKER PATH
Client upload
→
FastAPI
→
Kafka
Consumer
→
Groq extraction
→
Pydantic + policy
MySQL state
→
Review / HubSpot handoff

Root-cause lens

If uploads start timing out during a model slowdown, I would first separate API latency from consumer lag. Check request traces, Kafka consumer-group lag, worker duration, provider errors and claim-state transitions before changing concurrency.

  • Decouple: accept and validate the upload, persist its tracking state, enqueue work and return a claim reference instead of waiting for inference.
  • Protect correctness: validate model output against a strict schema, then run deterministic policy checks. A valid JSON response is not automatically a valid claim.
  • Recover safely: define retryable versus permanent failures, cap retries, isolate poison jobs and make claim-state transitions explicit before replaying work.
Key system-design decision

Kafka absorbs bursts and separates request handling from expensive extraction. The API stays responsive while the worker pipeline owns the longer-running workflow. Retry limits, dead-letter handling and replay controls are hardening considerations, not claims about existing repository implementation.

02 / REVIEWGUARD · DISTRIBUTED TASK ORCHESTRATION

How do you make webhook retries safe when workers can crash?

Webhook delivery is at-least-once in practice. A timeout does not tell the sender whether the application accepted the event, and a worker retry can repeat an external side effect.

EVENT LIFECYCLE / IDEMPOTENT PROCESSING
WhatsApp event
→
FastAPI webhook
Redis dedup key
→
Celery queue
→
LangGraph
Persist decision
→
Safe reply / support route

Root-cause lens

I would trace one provider message ID across webhook logs, Redis, Celery task IDs, workflow decisions and outbound provider responses. This identifies whether duplication began at ingress, task execution or message sending.

  • Ingress: acknowledge quickly and use the provider's stable event ID as an idempotency key so a retry does not enqueue a second logical job.
  • Execution: persist processing state and make task handlers safe to retry; do not assume Celery's delivery semantics create exactly-once business behaviour.
  • Side effects: track outbound send state separately. If the provider accepted a message but the worker crashed before recording success, reconcile delivery before retrying.
Key system-design decision

Separate event receipt, AI decision-making and outbound delivery into distinct stages. That makes each boundary observable and gives the system a place to resolve uncertain outcomes rather than blindly repeating a customer-facing action.

PROJECT STACK · FastAPI · Celery · Redis · LangGraph · 71 offline tests. Provider-specific idempotency and delivery reconciliation depend on API support.

03 / PDF SAHAKARI · RETRIEVAL SYSTEM DESIGN

How do you prevent a RAG pipeline from returning a plausible but unsupported answer?

Vector similarity is only a retrieval signal. Similar wording, missing page structure or poor chunk boundaries can put the wrong evidence in the model context.

RETRIEVAL → EVIDENCE → RESPONSE
PDF ingestion
→
Chunk + metadata
Vertex embeddings
→
Pinecone search
→
Context assembly
Mixtral response
→
Grounded answer / abstain

Root-cause lens

Debug retrieval and generation separately. Inspect the retrieved chunk text, page metadata and ranking before reading the final answer. If the evidence is absent, prompt changes cannot repair the retrieval layer.

  • Ingestion: preserve page numbers, headings and useful document structure; tune chunk size and overlap around the source material.
  • Retrieval: evaluate whether the expected passage appears in top-k results. Add metadata filtering or reranking only when the evaluation set shows a measurable benefit.
  • Generation: constrain answers to supplied evidence, expose source references and abstain when the retrieved context cannot support the requested claim.
Key system-design decision

Treat retrieval quality as an independently testable subsystem. Measure Recall@k, answer correctness and faithfulness separately, and include unanswerable questions so the system is rewarded for saying “not found” when appropriate.

PROJECT STACK · LangChain · Pinecone · Vertex AI embeddings · Mixtral 8x7B · Streamlit
